title: Any wood makes fire
hookLine: a young brahmin argues caste; fire from any wood burns the same

lines: DON'T BE BEATEN WITHOUT A FIGHT.
cards: Five hundred brahmins are staying in Sāvatthī, and they're worried. This Gotama is teaching that all four classes can be purified. Someone has to go and argue with him.
They choose Assalāyana, sixteen years old, brilliant, already a master of the old texts. He doesn't want to go. The Buddha speaks the Dhamma, he says, and someone who does is hard to argue with.
They insist: don't be beaten without a fight. So a sixteen-year-old walks in to debate the Buddha, carrying his elders' claim on his shoulders.

teach.b: Assalāyana states the claim as the brahmins of that time held it: brahmins are the highest class, born of Brahmā, from his mouth. The Buddha's first answer is almost blunt.
Brahmin women are seen menstruating, pregnant, giving birth and nursing. Brahmins are born from wombs like everyone else. Then he widens the view.

teach.h: ONLY TWO CLASSES IN THE NORTHWEST.
teach.b: In the lands to the northwest, among the Greeks and Kambojans, there are only two classes, masters and servants, and people move from one to the other. So the four-class order isn't a law of nature. Then gentler tests.
Can only a brahmin develop a mind of loving-kindness? No, all four classes can.

teach.h: ANYONE CAN BATHE IN THE RIVER.
teach.b: Can only a brahmin take a back scrubber and bath powder to the river and get clean? No, anyone can. And then the fire.
Suppose, the Buddha says, a king gathers a hundred men of different births. Those of high birth make fire with fine woods: sal, pine, lotus, sandalwood.

Those of low birth use scraps from a dog's trough, a pig's trough, a washerman's tub, castor-oil wood. Would one fire have flame and color and light, and the other not? Would one cook food and the other not?
Fire is fire. Whatever the wood, it burns the same and gives the same heat. By the end the young man sits silent, head bowed, and goes for refuge.
The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "I do not call a man a Brâhmana because of his origin or of his mother." In the Buddhist texts, the word is kept, and given to conduct.

how: Buddhist communities ordain people of every background, and teachers in South Asia, including the movement led by B. R. Ambedkar, have drawn on suttas like this one in rejecting discrimination by birth.

o: a sacred flame only priests may light
the sandalwood burned in a temple
fire, the same whatever wood it burns

games.q: the Buddha's answers to Assalāyana: tap the pairs.
p: only masters and servants, who switch

s: Assalāyana was eager to debate the Buddha
he didn't want to go; the other brahmins insisted.
the Buddha points out that brahmins are born from wombs like everyone
he mentions brahmin women menstruating, pregnant and nursing.
in the fire test, fire from fine wood burns brighter
Assalāyana admits that fire from any wood has the same flame, color and heat.

games.q: a king has a hundred men of different births make fires: some from sandalwood, some from a pig's trough. which fire cooks the food?
o: only the fire of the high-born
games.why: Assalāyana himself admits it: whatever the wood, fire burns the same and serves the same purpose.

practice: If you have a match or a lighter nearby and it's safe, strike it and watch the flame for a breath or two, then put it out; if not, picture a small flame, and notice that you can't tell what box it came from.
Then bring to mind someone you tend to rank below or above you, and picture the same flame in them.

wordCard.voice: Aggi. Sandalwood or a pig's trough, fire gives the same light and heat. The Buddha's answer to a sixteen-year-old about birth and worth.

orig.note: Pali aggi (Sanskrit agni): fire. the image at the heart of the sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: fire is fire. Sandalwood or scraps, the same light. That's day four hundred seventy-five.
